entries.meaning: A system of tracks and trains, or the company that operates it. ---
examples: The old railway ran straight through the middle of town.
Several railways merged into one company in the 1970s.
A narrow railway still climbs to the summit every summer.
entries.contrast: Americans normally say railroad; railway survives mainly in company names and in British English.

entries.meaning: One of the two steel bars a train runs on, or train transportation taken as a whole. ---
examples: A crew replaced a cracked rail just south of the bridge.
Two steel rails ran straight out to the horizon.
We shipped the whole load by rail instead of by truck.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The business and work of running railroads. ---
examples: He spent forty years in railroading before he retired.
Railroading was dangerous work in those days.
Her grandfather taught her everything he knew about railroading.
entries.русский: железнодорожное дело, работа на железной дороге

entries.meaning: The pair of rails, with their ties and ballast, that a train runs on. ---
examples: Our house sits about a hundred yards from the railroad tracks.
Kids are told never to play on the railroad track.
Weeds had grown up between the railroad tracks.
entries.contrast: Americans say railroad track; the British say railway line.

entries.meaning: A crossing where the road and the track meet at the same level. ---
examples: The state is paying to eliminate two dangerous grade crossings.
A truck stalled on the grade crossing and had to be towed off.
Most accidents happen at grade crossings without gates.
entries.contrast: Americans say grade crossing; the British say level crossing.

entries.meaning: The striped arm that drops to stop traffic before a train passes. ---
examples: The crossing gate came down and the bell started ringing.
Someone drove around the crossing gates and was nearly hit.
Both crossing gates were stuck in the up position.

entries.meaning: The white X-shaped sign that marks a railroad crossing. ---
examples: A faded crossbuck was the only warning at that crossing.
The county replaced the old crossbucks with flashing lights.
You could barely read the crossbuck in the dark.

entries.meaning: The bell that rings to warn drivers that a train is coming. ---
examples: The crossing bell woke us up at two in the morning.
You can hear the crossing bells from our back porch.
The crossing bell kept clanging long after the train had gone.

entries.meaning: A train that carries goods rather than passengers. ---
examples: A mile-long freight train blocked the road for twenty minutes.
Freight trains run through here all night.
The freight train was pulling more than a hundred cars.
entries.contrast: The gh in freight is silent: FRAYT, rhyming with eight.

entries.meaning: A train that carries people. ---
examples: Only two passenger trains a day stop in this town.
The passenger train pulled in right on time.
Freight moved aside to let the passenger train through.

entries.meaning: A short-distance train that carries people to and from work. ---
examples: I catch the 6:40 commuter train every weekday.
Commuter trains were packed after the game let out.
The commuter train stops at every station on the line.

entries.meaning: A fast train that skips most of the stops along the way. ---
examples: Take the express train if you want to get there by noon.
Two express trains an hour run between the cities.
The express train blew right past our platform.

entries.meaning: A train that stops at every station on its route. ---
examples: We missed the express and had to take the local train.
The local train takes almost twice as long.
Local trains run every half hour on weekends.

entries.meaning: A very fast passenger train built for long-distance travel. ---
examples: We took the bullet train from Tokyo to Kyoto.
Bullet trains can hit almost two hundred miles an hour.
A bullet train would cut the trip in half.

entries.meaning: A train pulled by a steam locomotive. ---
examples: The museum runs a steam train on summer weekends.
My grandfather remembers riding steam trains as a boy.
You could smell the steam train before you saw it.

entries.meaning: A train that runs overnight, usually with sleeping accommodations. ---
examples: We took the night train and woke up in Chicago.
Night trains are cheaper than flying if you can sleep sitting up.
The night train leaves at ten past eleven.

entries.meaning: Train service designed to run at very high speeds between cities. ---
examples: The state has been promising high-speed rail for twenty years.
High-speed rail would connect the two downtowns in an hour.
Voters approved funding for high-speed rail in 2008.

entries.meaning: A city rail system using smaller, lighter trains, often on street level. ---
examples: Light rail runs from the airport straight to the stadium.
The city is adding two new light rail stops downtown.
We take light rail whenever parking looks bad.

entries.meaning: Train service between a city and the suburbs around it. ---
examples: Commuter rail saved me an hour of driving each way.
The suburb grew up around a commuter rail stop.
Commuter rail service was suspended after the storm.

entries.meaning: Fast urban train service that runs on its own tracks, away from traffic. ---
examples: The region finally got rapid transit in the 1970s.
Rapid transit carries most of the downtown workforce.
They are studying rapid transit along the river corridor.

entries.meaning: Public transportation systems that move large numbers of people. ---
examples: The bill sets aside billions for mass transit.
Without mass transit this city would not function.
He has never owned a car and relies on mass transit.

entries.meaning: An underground stop where subway trains pick up passengers. ---
examples: There is a subway station two blocks from the apartment.
Three subway stations were closed for repairs.
Musicians play in the subway station every evening.

entries.meaning: One of the connected cars that make up a subway train. ---
examples: The last subway car is usually the emptiest.
New subway cars have wider doors and better lighting.
Someone was playing a saxophone in our subway car.

entries.meaning: One route of a subway system, usually known by a color, letter, or number. ---
examples: Take the blue subway line four stops north.
Two subway lines meet under the courthouse.
The new subway line opens next spring.

entries.meaning: A metal coin once bought to get through a subway turnstile. ---
examples: I still have a couple of old subway tokens in a drawer.
You used to drop a subway token into the slot.
Subway tokens were replaced by fare cards years ago.

entries.meaning: An urban underground railroad system. ---
examples: We bought a day pass for the metro.
The metro runs until one in the morning.
Several European metros are older than ours.
entries.contrast: Americans call their own systems the subway; metro is used mostly for foreign systems and for the one in Washington.

entries.meaning: A passenger car that runs on rails laid in a city street. ---
examples: A streetcar rattled past the corner every ten minutes.
The city tore up its streetcar lines in the 1950s.
We rode the streetcar down to the waterfront.
entries.contrast: American streetcar equals British tram.

entries.meaning: A streetcar, especially outside the United States. ---
examples: We took a tram from the station to the old town.
Trams in Lisbon climb some very steep streets.
The tram was crowded with tourists.
entries.contrast: Tram is the British word; Americans usually say streetcar or trolley.

entries.meaning: A city train that runs on tracks built above the street. ---
examples: An elevated train roared over our heads every few minutes.
Elevated trains cast long shadows across the avenue.
You can hear the elevated train from inside the restaurant.

entries.meaning: A train that floats above its guideway on magnets instead of rolling on rails. ---
examples: The maglev covers the thirty miles in about seven minutes.
Only a handful of maglevs are in service anywhere.
A maglev makes almost no noise at low speed.

entries.meaning: A short railway on a steep slope where two cars are pulled by a cable. ---
examples: A funicular carries visitors up to the observation deck.
The funicular has been running since 1901.
Both funiculars were closed for the winter.

entries.meaning: A mountain railway whose engine grips a toothed rail to climb steep grades. ---
examples: The cog railway takes about an hour to reach the summit.
Cog railways can climb slopes no ordinary train could manage.
We rode the cog railway up the mountain in the rain.

entries.meaning: A stretch of railroad running between two places. ---
examples: The rail line follows the river for thirty miles.
Two rail lines cross just north of the town.
That rail line has been abandoned since the mill closed.

entries.meaning: The principal route of a railroad, carrying most of its traffic. ---
examples: Freight rolls down the main line day and night.
The branch rejoins the main line at the junction.
Both main lines were shut down by the derailment.
entries.contrast: Written as one word, mainline, when it comes before a noun: mainline service.

entries.meaning: A secondary rail line that leaves the main route and serves smaller places. ---
examples: The branch line to the quarry closed in 1974.
Most branch lines in the county are gone now.
A single engine works the branch line twice a week.

entries.meaning: A short track leading off the main line to a factory, mine, or warehouse. ---
examples: A spur line runs right into the grain elevator.
They built a spur line to serve the new plant.
Two spur lines branch off just past the yard.

entries.meaning: All the connected rail lines of a country or region. ---
examples: The country has one of the densest rail networks in the world.
Storm damage shut down half the rail network.
Freight moves across the whole rail network without changing cars.

entries.meaning: The activity of going places by train. ---
examples: Rail travel is slower but far more comfortable than flying.
She writes a blog about rail travel in North America.
Rail travel picked up again after gas prices rose.
entries.contrast: Travel is uncountable here — never rail travels.

entries.meaning: Goods carried by train, or the business of carrying them. ---
examples: Rail freight is cheaper than trucking over long distances.
Most of the coal moves as rail freight.
The port handles both rail freight and containers.

entries.meaning: The movement of trains over a line or network. ---
examples: Rail traffic through the tunnel doubled in ten years.
The accident stopped all rail traffic for six hours.
Rail traffic is heaviest just before dawn.

entries.meaning: The strip of land a railroad owns and runs its tracks along. ---
examples: The company still owns the right-of-way through the valley.
Old rights-of-way have been turned into bike trails.
Fences run along both sides of the right-of-way.
entries.contrast: The plural puts the s in the middle: rights-of-way, not right-of-ways.

entries.meaning: A bridge built to carry train tracks over water, a road, or a valley. ---
examples: The old railroad bridge is still standing downstream.
Two railroad bridges cross the river within a mile.
They closed the railroad bridge for inspection.

entries.meaning: The big open hall of a station where passengers gather before boarding. ---
examples: We met under the clock in the main concourse.
The concourse was jammed with holiday travelers.
Both concourses have been restored to their original look.

entries.meaning: A room at a station where passengers sit until their train arrives. ---
examples: We sat in the waiting room with our bags for two hours.
The waiting room has wooden benches and a coal stove.
Small stations rarely keep their waiting rooms open at night.

entries.meaning: The place in a station where tickets are sold. ---
examples: The ticket office opens half an hour before the first train.
Ask at the ticket office about the student discount.
Many small-town ticket offices have closed for good.

entries.meaning: The counter opening where a clerk sells tickets. ---
examples: There was one clerk working and four ticket windows closed.
He slid the money under the ticket window.
The line at the ticket window went out the door.

entries.meaning: A machine that sells tickets without a clerk. ---
examples: The ticket machine on the platform takes cards only.
Two of the three ticket machines were out of order.
Buy at the ticket machine if the office is closed.

entries.meaning: A railroad employee who sells tickets and answers travel questions. ---
examples: The ticket agent found us a cheaper connection.
Ticket agents here know every schedule by heart.
Ask the ticket agent which track the train leaves from.

entries.meaning: The barrier you tap or swipe a card at to enter a transit system. ---
examples: The fare gate wouldn't open, so I tapped again.
New fare gates are being installed at every station.
He got stuck at the fare gate with his suitcase.

entries.meaning: A card you load with money and use to pay for train or subway rides. ---
examples: I need to put more money on my fare card.
Fare cards replaced tokens about twenty years ago.
Tap your fare card on the round reader.

entries.meaning: The big screen or sign listing trains and the times they leave. ---
examples: Everyone stood staring up at the departure board.
The departure board still showed our train as on time.
Both departure boards went blank during the outage.

entries.meaning: The number identifying which track a train will leave from. ---
examples: They don't post the track number until ten minutes before departure.
Check the track number on the board before you go down.
The track numbers changed twice while we waited.
entries.contrast: American stations announce a track number where British ones announce a platform number.

entries.meaning: A ticket that lets you ride as much as you like for a set period. ---
examples: We bought a two-week rail pass before we left.
Rail passes pay for themselves after about four trips.
Show your rail pass to the conductor when he comes by.

entries.meaning: The shelf above the seats where passengers put their bags. ---
examples: He lifted the suitcase onto the luggage rack.
Every luggage rack in the car was already full.
Don't leave anything on the luggage rack when you get off.
entries.contrast: Luggage itself is uncountable — two pieces of luggage, never two luggages.

entries.meaning: A lot where drivers leave their cars and finish the trip by train. ---
examples: I leave the car at the park-and-ride and take the 7:15.
The park-and-ride fills up by seven in the morning.
Three new park-and-rides opened along the line.

entries.meaning: The number of people who use a train or transit system. ---
examples: Ridership fell sharply during the pandemic.
Weekend ridership is about half what it is on weekdays.
The new line boosted ridership along the whole corridor.

entries.meaning: A standing passenger on a crowded subway or streetcar. ---
examples: A car full of tired straphangers swayed with every curve.
As a daily straphanger, she knows exactly where to stand.
Straphangers were packed in shoulder to shoulder.

entries.meaning: Someone whose hobby is watching, photographing, and studying trains. ---
examples: Railfans line the bridge whenever the steam engine runs.
He's been a railfan since he was six.
A few railfans had set up cameras along the curve.

entries.meaning: A small working copy of a real train, used for a hobby layout. ---
examples: His basement is filled with model trains and tiny towns.
She bought him a model train for his birthday.
Model trains from the 1950s can be worth real money.

entries.meaning: A toy engine with cars and a loop of track, sold as one package. ---
examples: We set up the train set around the Christmas tree.
His first train set is still in the attic.
Most train sets come with a circle of track and a transformer.

entries.meaning: A trip taken on a train. ---
examples: It's a four-hour train ride to the coast.
The kids loved the train ride more than the museum.
We took two long train rides on that vacation.

entries.meaning: The paper or digital pass that lets you ride a particular train. ---
examples: I bought our train tickets online last night.
Keep your train ticket until you leave the station.
He lost his train ticket somewhere on the platform.

entries.meaning: The price charged for riding a train. ---
examples: The train fare went up again in January.
Train fares are cheaper if you book two weeks ahead.
Round-trip train fare comes to about forty dollars.

entries.meaning: The long warning sound a locomotive makes, especially near crossings. ---
examples: You could hear the train whistle across the whole valley.
A train whistle woke me at four in the morning.
Train whistles are still my favorite sound.
entries.contrast: The t in whistle is silent: WISS-uhl.

entries.meaning: The loud air horn a modern locomotive sounds as a warning. ---
examples: The train horn blasted twice before the crossing.
Neighbors petitioned to have the train horns silenced at night.
A train horn can be heard for more than a mile.

entries.meaning: A serious crash involving a train. ---
examples: Twelve people were hurt in the train wreck outside Denver.
The museum has photographs of famous train wrecks.
Investigators spent a week at the site of the train wreck.
entries.contrast: The w in wreck is silent: REK.

entries.meaning: A very small town where trains stop only when signaled. ---
examples: He grew up in a whistle-stop on the Kansas plains.
The candidate made a dozen whistle-stops in two days.
That whistle-stop has one store and a grain elevator.
entries.contrast: The t in whistle is silent: WISS-uhl STAHP.

entries.meaning: A small stop between the main stations on a line. ---
examples: The train pauses at half a dozen way stations.
This way station is little more than a shelter and a bench.
Freight rarely stops at the smaller way stations.

entries.meaning: All the engines and cars a railroad owns. ---
examples: Half the company's rolling stock is more than thirty years old.
They are spending millions to replace aging rolling stock.
The yard was full of idle rolling stock.
entries.contrast: Rolling stock is uncountable — never rolling stocks.

entries.meaning: An engine that burns coal or oil to make steam and pull a train. ---
examples: A restored steam locomotive pulls the excursion train.
Steam locomotives disappeared from most lines by 1960.
The steam locomotive needed water every fifty miles.

entries.meaning: An engine powered by a diesel motor that drives electric traction motors. ---
examples: Four diesel locomotives were needed to get the train over the pass.
The diesel locomotive idled for an hour in the yard.
Diesel locomotives replaced steam after the war.

entries.meaning: An engine that draws power from an overhead wire or a third rail. ---
examples: An electric locomotive took over at the state line.
Electric locomotives accelerate much faster than diesels.
The electric locomotive ran silently out of the tunnel.

entries.meaning: A machine driven by steam pressure, especially an old railroad engine. ---
examples: The steam engine hissed and slowly began to move.
Two steam engines are kept in working order here.
A steam engine takes hours to build up pressure.

entries.meaning: A small locomotive used to move cars around inside a yard. ---
examples: A switch engine shoved the cars onto the far track.
Two switch engines work the yard around the clock.
The switch engine never leaves the terminal.

entries.meaning: Any single vehicle that runs on rails as part of a train. ---
examples: The train was made up of eighty railroad cars.
One railroad car had jumped the track.
They restored a wooden railroad car from the 1890s.

entries.meaning: A railroad car built to carry goods rather than people. ---
examples: Rusting freight cars sat on the siding for years.
Each freight car holds about a hundred tons.
They loaded the lumber into an open freight car.
entries.contrast: American freight car equals British goods wagon.

entries.meaning: A railroad car fitted with seats for travelers. ---
examples: The train had six passenger cars and a baggage car.
Our passenger car was less than half full.
Older passenger cars had windows you could open.

entries.meaning: A railroad car where meals are cooked and served. ---
examples: We had breakfast in the dining car somewhere in Nebraska.
The dining car opens for dinner at five thirty.
Dining cars used to have white tablecloths and real silver.

entries.meaning: A railroad car with beds for overnight passengers. ---
examples: We booked a room in the sleeping car for the trip west.
Both sleeping cars were sold out weeks ahead.
The sleeping car attendant made up our beds after dinner.

entries.meaning: A sleeping car, or a train that has one. ---
examples: We took the sleeper from Chicago to Los Angeles.
There were two sleepers at the back of the train.
A berth in the sleeper costs about twice the coach fare.
entries.contrast: In American English a sleeper is a sleeping car; in British English a sleeper is also a railroad tie.

entries.meaning: A railroad car with large windows for looking at the scenery. ---
examples: We spent the afternoon in the observation car.
The observation car fills up as soon as the mountains appear.
Old observation cars had a platform at the back.
entries.русский: смотровой вагон, вагон с панорамными окнами

entries.meaning: A railroad car that carries suitcases, boxes, and bicycles. ---
examples: Skis have to go in the baggage car.
The baggage car is right behind the engine.
Two baggage cars were added for the holiday rush.

entries.meaning: A railroad car in which mail was carried and sorted along the way. ---
examples: Clerks sorted letters in the mail car as the train ran.
The last mail cars came off the trains in the 1970s.
A restored mail car stands at the far end of the museum.

entries.meaning: A railroad car with comfortable chairs where drinks and snacks are sold. ---
examples: He bought a coffee in the club car.
The club car is three cars forward.
Club cars on the commuter line stay busy on Friday nights.

entries.meaning: A car where phone calls and loud conversation are not allowed. ---
examples: I always try to get a seat in the quiet car.
Someone took a call in the quiet car and got glared at.
Most morning trains have one quiet car.

entries.meaning: A freight car shaped like a cylinder for carrying liquids or gases. ---
examples: A string of black tank cars rolled past the crossing.
The tank car was carrying corn syrup.
New tank cars have thicker shells for safety.

entries.meaning: A freight car that dumps loose cargo through doors in its floor. ---
examples: Coal is hauled in open hopper cars.
The hopper car emptied its grain in under a minute.
Sixty hopper cars were waiting at the elevator.

entries.meaning: An open freight car with low sides, used for scrap, steel, or gravel. ---
examples: Scrap metal was piled high in the gondola cars.
A single gondola car sat on the siding.
They loaded rail into gondola cars with a crane.
entries.contrast: Stress the first syllable: GAHN-duh-luh, the same as the Venetian boat.

entries.meaning: An insulated freight car that keeps food cold in transit. ---
examples: Oranges traveled east in refrigerator cars packed with ice.
The refrigerator car broke down and the load was lost.
Refrigerator cars changed what Americans could eat in winter.

entries.meaning: A slatted freight car used to haul livestock. ---
examples: They drove the steers up a ramp into the cattle car.
Old cattle cars rot in the weeds behind the stockyard.
A cattle car had to be cleaned out after every trip.

entries.meaning: A freight car with no sides or roof, used for long or bulky loads. ---
examples: Two bulldozers were chained to a flatcar.
Lumber rides east on flatcars.
The flatcar carried a single enormous turbine.

entries.meaning: The car behind a steam locomotive that carries its fuel and water. ---
examples: The fireman shoveled coal from the tender all night.
The engine and its tender weigh over two hundred tons.
Both tenders were repainted for the excursion.

entries.meaning: The angled frame on the front of a locomotive that pushes obstacles off the track. ---
examples: A branch got caught in the cowcatcher.
Early locomotives had big iron cowcatchers.
He posed for a photograph sitting on the cowcatcher.

entries.meaning: The chamber in a steam locomotive where the fuel burns. ---
examples: He opened the firebox and the cab filled with light.
The firebox has to be cleaned out after every run.
Cracks in the firebox took the engine out of service.

entries.meaning: One of the large powered wheels that push a locomotive along. ---
examples: The driving wheels were taller than a man.
A slipping driving wheel threw sparks along the rail.
This engine has six driving wheels on each side.

entries.meaning: The swiveling frame of wheels under each end of a railroad car. ---
examples: A cracked bogie took the car out of service.
Each coach rides on two bogies.
The bogie turns to let the car follow a curve.
entries.contrast: American railroaders usually say truck; bogie is the British word.

entries.meaning: The hooked device that locks one railroad car to the next. ---
examples: The coupler snapped shut with a heavy clang.
A broken coupler left half the train behind.
Modern couplers lock automatically on contact.

entries.meaning: A braking system that uses compressed air to stop every car in a train. ---
examples: You could hear the air brakes hiss as the train slowed.
The air brake made long freight trains far safer.
He tested the air brakes before leaving the yard.

entries.meaning: A bed built into the wall of a sleeping car. ---
examples: I had the upper berth and slept badly.
The compartment has two berths and a small sink.
He folded the berth back against the wall.
entries.contrast: Berth sounds exactly like birth.

entries.meaning: As much cargo or as many people as one train can carry. ---
examples: A trainload of coal leaves the mine every morning.
They shipped three trainloads of grain last week.
A whole trainload of soldiers came through the station.

entries.meaning: The amount of freight that fills one railroad car. ---
examples: The mill ships forty carloads of paper a month.
Rates are lower if you order a full carload.
One carload of lumber was damaged in the storm.

entries.meaning: One of the heavy wooden or concrete beams that hold the rails in place. ---
examples: They stacked old railroad ties beside the track.
Each railroad tie is soaked in creosote to keep it from rotting.
We used railroad ties to build a retaining wall.
entries.contrast: Also called a crosstie in the United States; the British word is sleeper.

entries.meaning: A railroad tie, laid crosswise under the rails. ---
examples: The crew replaced two hundred rotten crossties.
Every crosstie is spiked down at both ends.
Grass had grown over the crossties.

entries.meaning: The crushed stone spread under and around railroad ties to hold the track steady. ---
examples: Fresh ballast was dumped along the whole stretch of track.
Rain washed the ballast out from under the rails.
The train hauls ballast to wherever the crews are working.
entries.contrast: Ballast is uncountable — a load of ballast, never two ballasts.

entries.meaning: The prepared ground and ballast that the track is laid on. ---
examples: Flooding washed away a hundred feet of roadbed.
A solid roadbed keeps the ride smooth.
Old roadbeds often become hiking trails.

entries.meaning: A bridge of braced timber or steel frames carrying track over a valley. ---
examples: The train crawled across the wooden trestle.
Two trestles burned in the forest fire.
That trestle is a hundred feet above the creek.
entries.contrast: The t before the l is silent: TRES-uhl.

entries.meaning: The electrified rail beside the track that powers a subway or commuter train. ---
examples: Never step onto the tracks — the third rail is live.
Ice on the third rail delayed the morning trains.
Workers shut off the third rail before going down.

entries.meaning: The electric line strung above the track that a train draws power from. ---
examples: A fallen tree brought down the overhead wire.
The overhead wires hum faintly in cold weather.
Streetcars draw current from an overhead wire.

entries.meaning: The hinged arm on the roof of an electric train that touches the overhead wire. ---
examples: The pantograph slid up against the wire with a spark.
Both pantographs are lowered before the train enters the shed.
A bent pantograph stopped service for an hour.

entries.meaning: The work of converting a rail line to run on electric power. ---
examples: Electrification of the corridor will take another six years.
The railroad put off electrification until the 1930s.
Electrification cuts both fuel costs and noise.

entries.meaning: The distance between the two rails of a track. ---
examples: The two railroads used different track gauges.
Track gauge here is four feet eight and a half inches.
Changing the track gauge meant relaying every mile.
entries.contrast: Gauge is spelled with -au- but sounds like GAYJ.

entries.meaning: A track width smaller than the standard one, used on cheap or mountain lines. ---
examples: The mining railroad was built to narrow gauge.
Several narrow gauges were once in use in Colorado.
A narrow gauge line still runs up the canyon.

entries.meaning: The track width used by most railroads, four feet eight and a half inches. ---
examples: Almost every line in North America is standard gauge.
The branch was rebuilt to standard gauge in 1902.
Standard gauge lets cars run from one railroad to another.

entries.meaning: A thick nail driven through the rail's base into the tie. ---
examples: He found a rusty railroad spike along the tracks.
Crews once drove railroad spikes by hand all day long.
A single railroad spike weighs about a pound.

entries.meaning: An area of many parallel tracks where trains are stored and made up. ---
examples: The rail yard stretches for two miles along the river.
Engines idle all night in the rail yard.
Both rail yards were built when the mills were running.

entries.meaning: A yard where freight cars are sorted onto tracks by destination. ---
examples: Cars are pushed over a hump in the classification yard.
The classification yard handles two thousand cars a day.
Big classification yards run twenty-four hours.

entries.meaning: A circular engine shed built around a turntable. ---
examples: The old roundhouse now holds a railroad museum.
Engines were serviced in the roundhouse between runs.
Only a few roundhouses are still standing.

entries.meaning: A rotating platform used to turn a locomotive around. ---
examples: They ran the engine onto the turntable and swung it around.
The turntable still works after ninety years.
Two men could turn the turntable by hand.

entries.meaning: A numbered post beside the track showing the distance along the line. ---
examples: The derailment happened near milepost 214.
Crews report their location by milepost.
White mileposts stand every mile along the right-of-way.

entries.meaning: An old signal with a movable arm that tells the engineer to stop or go. ---
examples: The semaphore dropped to clear and the train moved on.
A few semaphores still stand on this branch.
The arm of the semaphore was frozen in place.

entries.meaning: A colored lamp beside the track telling a train whether it may proceed. ---
examples: The signal light went from red to green.
Signal lights glowed along the curve in the fog.
He slowed down at the first signal light.

entries.meaning: A signal that keeps only one train at a time inside a section of track. ---
examples: The block signal stayed red until the section cleared.
Block signals prevent one train from catching another.
A failed block signal forced the train to a crawl.

entries.meaning: A small building from which switches and signals are worked. ---
examples: A man in the signal box pulled a row of long levers.
The signal box at the junction was torn down last year.
Old signal boxes have been replaced by one control center.
entries.contrast: Signal box is the British term; Americans usually say interlocking tower.

entries.meaning: A system of switches and signals wired so no two conflicting routes can be set. ---
examples: The interlocking at the junction was rebuilt last summer.
An interlocking makes it impossible to line up two trains for the same track.
Several interlockings are now controlled from one office.

entries.meaning: An accident in which a train comes off the track. ---
examples: The derailment closed the line for three days.
No one was hurt in the derailment.
Two derailments in one month brought in federal inspectors.

entries.meaning: A small open car pushed along the rails by pumping a handle. ---
examples: Two workers pumped the handcar down the line.
The museum lets kids ride a handcar on a short track.
Handcars were how section crews got to work.

entries.meaning: A short second track where one train waits for another to go by. ---
examples: We sat in a passing siding for twenty minutes.
The railroad is adding passing sidings to speed things up.
Only one passing siding is left on this stretch.

entries.meaning: The workers who repair and maintain the rails, ties, and ballast. ---
examples: A track crew was replacing ties near the bridge.
Track crews work through the night to avoid delays.
The track crew flagged our train down to a walking pace.

entries.meaning: The person who drives a train. ---
examples: The locomotive engineer sounded the horn at every crossing.
Locomotive engineers train for years before they run alone.
His father was a locomotive engineer on this same line.
entries.contrast: Americans call this person an engineer; the British say engine driver.

entries.meaning: The operator of a subway train or a streetcar. ---
examples: The motorman leaned out and looked back along the platform.
Motormen on this line work eight-hour shifts.
A new motorman was at the controls.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: one motorman, two motormen.

entries.meaning: A crew member who works the brakes, switches, and couplings on a train. ---
examples: The brakeman climbed down to throw the switch.
Two brakemen rode in the caboose.
He started out as a brakeman at nineteen.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: one brakeman, two brakemen.

entries.meaning: The person in charge of a railroad station. ---
examples: The stationmaster unlocked the waiting room at dawn.
Ask the stationmaster where to leave the trunk.
Stationmasters used to live upstairs over the depot.

entries.meaning: The person who runs a rail yard and directs the switching crews. ---
examples: The yardmaster decided which cars went out first.
Radios crackle in the yardmaster's tower all night.
Two yardmasters split the twenty-four-hour shift.

entries.meaning: A yard worker who throws switches to move cars from track to track. ---
examples: The switchman signaled with a lantern.
Three switchmen worked the night shift.
A switchman rides the side of the car as it rolls.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: one switchman, two switchmen.

entries.meaning: A worker who operates or maintains railroad signals. ---
examples: The signalman worked the levers from the tower.
Signalmen were called out to fix the frozen switch.
A signalman checked every lamp along the line.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: one signalman, two signalmen.

entries.meaning: A crew member who walks back with a flag or lantern to warn other trains. ---
examples: The flagman went back half a mile to protect the train.
Two flagmen stood at either end of the work zone.
The flagman waved us through at a slow speed.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: one flagman, two flagmen.

entries.meaning: Someone who works for a railroad. ---
examples: Three generations of railroaders have lived in that house.
Old railroaders gather at the diner every morning.
He was a railroader his whole working life.

entries.meaning: A porter who carries passengers' bags at a railroad station.
examples: A redcap wheeled our suitcases to the platform.
Redcaps met every long-distance train.
He tipped the redcap five dollars.
